reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods
chapter_title: Placement and Design of Concrete for Drilled Shafts

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Construction of a drilled shaft foundation is essentially fabrication of a reinforced concrete structure in-situ, often under extremely challenging conditions with underwater placement at depths exceeding 100 ft. Concrete placement techniques and materials are critical and require thorough planning and design. The mix design and method of placement are most often delegated to the contractor with submittals required for approval.
key_points: Concrete placement is a critical aspect of drilled shaft construction
Mix design is typically delegated to the contractor with engineer approval
Chapter focuses on workability characteristics critical for construction success
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft construction projects requiring concrete placement

sections.title: Basic Characteristics of Drilled Shaft Concrete
sections.body: Drilled shaft concrete must meet unique requirements compared to other reinforced concrete structures. The key properties are: filling ability (flow through tremie and fill excavation), passing ability (flow through reinforcement without blocking), self-weight compaction (consolidate without vibration), resistance to segregation and bleeding, resistance to leaching, controlled setting (retain workability during placement), durability, low heat of hydration (for large diameters), and appropriate strength and stiffness.
key_points: Concrete must self-consolidate under its own weight without vibration
Must remain fluid for 4 to 8 hours under varying temperature conditions
Filling ability and passing ability are the most critical fresh properties
Compressive strengths of 4,000 to 5,000 psi are typical
sections.applicability: Specifying and evaluating concrete for drilled shaft construction

sections.title: Placement of Concrete
sections.body: Concrete placement must be carefully planned for the specific construction method (dry, cased, or wet). In dry excavations, concrete can be placed by free fall up to 80 ft without problems as long as it does not strike the cage or borehole wall. In cased holes, the concrete head must exceed external fluid pressure during casing extraction. In wet excavations, tremie or pump placement is required with minimum 10 ft embedment maintained in fresh concrete.
key_points: Free fall placement acceptable up to 80 ft if concrete does not strike cage or walls
Depth-to-cage-diameter ratio of 24 or less allows free fall without problems
Water inflow exceeding 12 inches per hour (1 inch per 5 min) requires wet method
Tremie must be embedded minimum 10 ft into fresh concrete during placement
Concrete head inside casing must exceed external fluid pressure during extraction
Bottom sediment should not exceed 3 inches prior to concrete placement

sections.title: Drilling Near a Recently Concreted Shaft
sections.body: Concrete in a recently placed shaft must achieve initial set before drilling or casing installation within a clear spacing of three shaft diameters. The primary concern is communication between excavations where fresh concrete could break through. A typical concrete mix achieves set within 24 hours; high-early-strength cement is not recommended for shafts exceeding 5 ft diameter due to heat of hydration concerns.
key_points: Minimum clear spacing of three shaft diameters before nearby drilling
Concrete must achieve initial set before nearby construction
Vibro-driving of casing near fresh concrete can create elevated pore pressures
Studies show vibration from nearby construction does not normally damage fresh concrete
sections.applicability: Construction sequencing for closely-spaced drilled shafts

sections.title: Base Grouting
sections.body: Post-grouting of the shaft base enhances end bearing and compensates for loose material at the bottom. Grout is delivered via tubes placed within the reinforcement using a neat water-cement mixture with w/c ratio of 0.40 to 0.55. Typical grouting pressures range up to 800 psi. Grouting is performed after concrete achieves at least 2500 psi compressive strength. Performance targets include achieving a minimum target pressure with a minimum grout volume and an upper limit on upward shaft movement.
key_points: Enhances end bearing capacity and compensates for base loosening
Grout is neat water-cement mixture with w/c ratio 0.40 to 0.55
Typical grouting pressures up to 800 psi
Performed after concrete achieves minimum 2500 psi
Multiple grout circuits provide redundancy against blockage
Upper limit on shaft upward movement; excessive volume indicates hydraulic fracture
figures: Figure 9-19: Sleeve Port Systems for Distribution of Grout to the Base
sections.applicability: Drilled shafts where enhanced end bearing is needed or base cleanliness is uncertain

sections.title: Concrete Mix Design
sections.body: The concrete mix must achieve properties needed for constructability while meeting structural requirements. Fresh concrete properties (workability, passing ability) are more critical than hardened properties for drilled shaft construction. Compressive strength requirements of 4,000 to 5,000 psi are typical and easily achieved with modern materials. The section covers cementitious materials, chemical admixtures, aggregate and water, workability, temperature control, and mixture proportions.
key_points: Type I or Type I/II Portland cement is standard; Type III should be avoided for shafts > 5 ft diameter
SCMs (fly ash, slag cement, silica fume) improve durability and reduce heat of hydration
Class C fly ash: 20-30% replacement; Class F fly ash: 15-25%; Slag: 30-50%; Silica fume: 5-8%
Slump of 6+ inches for dry method, about 9 inches for wet/casing methods
Self-consolidating concrete (SCC) uses slump flow of 18-24 inches
Water/cementitious materials ratio (w/cm) of 0.40 to 0.45 typical; HRWR can reduce to 0.35
Maximum coarse aggregate size typically 3/4 inch; many agencies use 3/8 inch
Set-controlling admixtures should allow 2+ hours beyond estimated placement time
Shafts > 5 ft diameter may experience mass concrete thermal effects (DEF risk above 158 deg F)

sections.title: Concrete Tests
sections.body: Quality control testing includes trial mixture approval, batch plant tests, and jobsite tests. Trial batching should evaluate slump loss over time and develop full-scale technique shafts before production. Batch plant inspections verify component proportions (cementitious +/-1%, aggregates +/-2%, water +/-1%). Jobsite testing should include temperature, slump, air content (if required), and cylinder samples. For SCC, slump flow and VSI tests replace conventional slump testing.
key_points: Trial mixtures should develop slump loss curves; maintain 4+ inch slump at 4 hours
Full-scale technique shaft recommended before production
Minimum one set of cylinders per drilled shaft for quality assurance
SCC requires slump flow test (ASTM C 1611) and VSI rating of 1.5 or less
Static segregation test (ASTM C 1610) should not exceed 10%
Addition of water at jobsite generally not recommended but sometimes necessary
sections.applicability: Quality control and quality assurance during drilled shaft concrete operations

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Concrete placement is one of the most critical aspects of drilled shaft construction. This chapter covers placement techniques, mix design emphasizing fresh concrete properties for constructability, examples of successful mix designs, and quality control testing procedures.
key_points: Workability is the most critical concrete property for drilled shafts
Mix design should prioritize fresh properties over hardened properties
Quality control testing is essential at batch plant and jobsite
sections.applicability: Overview and summary of drilled shaft concrete requirements
